title: What to think about when improvising: learn the language
summary: He says improvisation starts from vocabulary and listening to the band, comparing music to language and medicine, and urges drawing on Parker, Young, Coltrane and others.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Um hum. Occasionally I’ll have a student ask me what I’m thinking about when I improvise. And I usually have a sort of hard time actually answering the question.

Because I think I’m fairly much chord oriented. I’m thinking about what chord I’m playing at the same time I’m thinking about trying to create a nice melody over the top of it. But if they’re not that familiar with chord structure yet, I’m not sure what to say to them.

Well you’re right, you have to have some understanding of harmonically what’s going on. But I will say you try to learn all of these various techniques and your phrases that you’re learning and themes, and then hopefully you can go on stage with the clean slate. And then you can just create based on what is provided to you by your musical environment at that particular time. So the pianist is feeding you something, the bass player is feeding you something, and the drummer is feeding you something, and I’m, hopefully, having a conversation with these individuals as well, and obviously we all think the way we think. So in that way you start to build your themes, based on those ideas that are being, they’re coming to you from that which you already know and that which you are hopefully being willing to accept or be a part of, that’s going on around you. But obviously it starts with vocabulary. So it’s like a person wants to speak English. Well you can’t speak English unless you know the A-B-C’s, unless you know how sentences are put together. So there has to be a certain amount of study before you can involve yourself. So I would say to a person just start learning the language. Once you start learning the language then you will be able to converse. But you can’t converse until you know the words. And every music or every language has certain things that go into the music. If I wanted to wake up tomorrow and be a rapper, there’s certain things that go with that diaspora that I have to study so that I will feel or be welcomed in as part of the clique. I hear people say well I don’t want to learn any of the things in the past because it’s going to hinder me. I don’t see how. It doesn’t hinder a doctor when he studies the history of music, I mean the history of medicine, to be a doctor. Nobody wants to go to a doctor that’s never studied any medicine. If you go to a doctor that says well I’m just doing my own thing, I’m not really going to use the history of medicine, nobody would go to that doctor. But all of a sudden when it comes to music, oh man, I’m going to do my own thing. Well you’re going to do your own thing, but it’s always going to come based on something, unless you’re just a hermit in the woods, and then all of a sudden you’re going to behave like an animal. Everybody has to cling, I feel, to something, to have a foundation. You’ve got to come from something. I mean we’re all born and we all

learn from somebody how we do what we do. Nobody just took a baby and just left them there, they wouldn’t make it. You’ve got to have some kind of development, so you’ve got to at some point recognize the techniques and use some part of the technique whether you want to come from the technique of Charlie Parker or you want to use the technique of Lester Young or you want to use the techniques used by Ornette Coleman or John Coltrane or Sun Ra or somebody. But you’ve got to pull from somewhere.
